The first thing I remember is a sound: not a voice, not exactly, but the way the air changed when a door shut. It wasn’t loud. It was decisive. After that, everything else in the room seemed to organize itself around absence—around the new fact that something had gone away and would not return at least for a while. I was too young to have words for that feeling, but I carried it anyway. Later, I’d learn that people make a whole language out of small departures. We call them goodbyes, deadlines, last chances, closures. Sometimes we even call them beginnings, which is a kinder way of admitting that something has ended.

I used to think endings were like cliffs. You’d walk, step, stumble, fall. But time doesn’t do that. Time slopes. It makes you believe you’re still walking forward, even as your foot finds the edge. A relationship ends not with fireworks but with a gradual thinning of shared attention. A childhood ends not with a dramatic scene but with the quiet realization that no one is coming to fetch you for something you used to be invited to. Even your own body—if you listen—translates its changes in soft increments. One morning you can’t hear a certain frequency. Another morning you can, but only with effort. The day you finally need glasses feels like an announcement, but the truth is that the announcement has been rehearsed in silence for years.

If I sound like I’m describing loss, it’s because I have always been fascinated by the ways we survive it. Survival is not always heroism. Most of the time it looks like ordinary routines. You wake up. You wash the same mug even though the tea tastes slightly different now. You learn to open a fridge without expecting to see someone else’s favorite food. You start telling new stories at the table, stories that have different endings.

And then there are the other kinds of change—the ones that don’t hurt so much, though they might still rearrange you. A new city. A new job. A new version of yourself that arrives not like a guest but like weather. It turns out you can be happy in unfamiliar places. You can learn the sound of a streetlamp clicking on at dusk. You can memorize how the morning light falls through the blinds in an apartment that isn’t yours. There’s a particular kind of courage in being willing to feel at home somewhere you haven’t earned yet. It’s an experiment in trust.

Sometimes I wonder whether adulthood is really about becoming steady, or whether it’s about becoming flexible. Steady sounds noble. Flexible sounds less impressive, but maybe it’s more accurate. The adult world doesn’t reward certainty as much as it rewards adaptation. You try. You fail, you try again. You learn that plans are weather forecasts and that you should pack an umbrella even on days that look clear. You learn that the skills you thought mattered might not, and the skills you ignored might become essential. You learn, slowly, that you can’t hold everything you want. You can only hold what fits in your hands and what doesn’t crush you.

That thought—what fits—has followed me into other places. I’ve tried to practice attention as if it were a craft. Attention is a strange substance. You can spend it, waste it, hoard it, give it away. When I was younger, I believed that attention was infinite. I believed I could focus on everything at once if I wanted enough. The older I get, the more I see attention as something like water: it always flows toward what the shape of the container allows. If the container is cluttered, the water splashes. If the container is shaped well, the water goes where you intend.

So I began to shape my days. Not with grand rules, not with the kind of discipline that looks good on posters, but with small choices that make it easier to stay human. I turn off notifications more often than I used to. I put my phone face down when I’m trying to read. I walk instead of scrolling sometimes, which feels like a betrayal at first because walking isn’t as immediately rewarding as swiping. But walking offers a different kind of reward: the world appears to you without being filtered into reaction buttons. You start noticing birds again. You start noticing that you can tell time by the angle of the sun. You start noticing your own body’s signals, which are easy to miss when you’re busy feeding them constant stimulation.

I’ve also learned that imagination is not just for artists or children. It’s a survival tool. It’s how you make a bridge between what is happening and what you can endure. When you’re stuck somewhere boring, imagination turns the minutes into material rather than punishment. When you’re stuck somewhere painful, imagination can be a rehearsal for the moment when the pain is no longer the center of your attention. The mind is not always a comfort, but it is always a generator of possibilities. Even when it’s producing worst-case scenarios, it’s still performing labor—trying to keep you alive by predicting threats.

There’s a darker version of this, of course. The mind can become a room you can’t find the exit to. It can trap you in loops: shame loop, regret loop, fear loop. I have lived in those rooms. The trick, I’ve found, is not to pretend the doors aren’t there. The trick is to decide what to do with them. Sometimes the best move is not to force your way out through brute will, but to sit down and wait for the loop to lose its grip. Sometimes the best move is to ask for help. Sometimes the best move is to do something physical—wash dishes, fold laundry, stretch—because your body can be an anchor even when your thoughts are storms.

What I’m circling, I think, is that life is mostly made of transitions. The day is a transition between morning and afternoon, between doing and resting, between one emotional temperature and another. People are transitions too: you meet them, you grow with them, you part. Sometimes you part with anger. Sometimes you part with love that can’t be expressed in the format you need. Sometimes you part quietly, like two shadows thinning at the edges of the same light. And what astonishes me is that despite all the departures, the world keeps making room. There is always another seat at the table. There is always another beginning somewhere, even if it isn’t the one you wanted.

Perhaps that’s the secret: not that loss doesn’t exist, but that it doesn’t get to be the only teacher. Life teaches by repetition and contrast. It teaches you what you can’t live without by testing it away. It teaches you what you can live with by showing you that survival is not a narrow path but a widening one. You become someone who can carry more than you expected. You become someone who can put down what used to weigh you down.

I don’t know where all this goes when I say it out loud. It could sound like philosophy, like a journal entry, like a message hidden in fog. But maybe it doesn’t need to land anywhere specific. Maybe it’s just a map of how I’ve moved through my own days—how I’ve listened to sounds like the closing door, how I’ve learned to recognize the slope of time, how I’ve practiced turning attention into a skill rather than a hope.

Tomorrow will be another transition. The air will change in small ways. Somewhere, a door will shut or a door will open. Someone will feel the room reorganize itself around absence or presence. And somewhere else, someone will discover that even when you don’t get what you thought you wanted, you can still live inside what you actually have—thread by thread, minute by minute, with the quiet insistence that the story is still being written.
